title: Health Assessment: Head-to-Toe Physical Assessment & Documentation
html:
A head-to-toe assessment is a systematic way to recognize the client's baseline, find meaningful change, and connect observations to safe nursing action. It is not a race to name every body part. The RN organizes the examination, protects privacy and comfort, compares findings, asks focused questions, identifies cues that cannot wait, and documents a useful clinical picture.

Learning goals

  • Prepare and sequence a respectful head-to-toe assessment.
  • Use inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation appropriately.
  • Recognize focused respiratory, cardiovascular, neurologic, integumentary, abdominal, and mobility cues.
  • Compare findings with baseline and between sides of the body when relevant.
  • Document objective findings, nursing actions, escalation, and reassessment.

Prepare the client and the setting

Review the reason for assessment, current diagnoses, recent procedures, orders, allergies, medications, trends, lines and devices, and prior findings. Introduce yourself, verify identity, explain what will happen, obtain permission before touch, provide privacy, and expose only the area being assessed. Hand hygiene, clean equipment, adequate lighting, a quiet environment, and warm hands all support accuracy and dignity.

Assessment is dynamic
Begin with airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, and immediate safety whenever the client appears unstable. A comprehensive sequence never replaces urgent focused assessment and escalation.

The core examination techniques

  • Inspection: observe appearance, symmetry, color, movement, devices, drainage, lesions, posture, work of breathing, and behavior.
  • Palpation: use touch to assess temperature, moisture, tenderness, texture, edema, pulses, masses, and crepitus when within nursing preparation and policy. Assess a painful area last.
  • Percussion: tap body surfaces to evaluate the character of underlying tissue; use it only when trained and appropriate for the setting.
  • Auscultation: listen to heart, lung, vascular, or bowel sounds in a quiet setting with the stethoscope directly on skin when appropriate.

For most body systems, use inspection, palpation, percussion, then auscultation as indicated. The abdomen is the important exception: inspect, auscultate, percuss, then palpate. Palpation or percussion before listening can alter bowel sounds and increase discomfort.

Work from general to focused

Use an organized order that fits the client and the setting. Start with general appearance and vital-sign trends, then assess head and neck, respiratory, cardiovascular/peripheral vascular, abdomen and elimination, musculoskeletal function and mobility, neurologic status, skin, and devices or wounds. A client cannot always tolerate the textbook order; adapt the sequence while preserving safety and clear documentation.

Respiratory and cardiovascular cues

Observe respiratory rate, rhythm, depth, effort, chest movement, ability to speak, cough, skin color, oxygen device and settings. Auscultate systematically side-to-side when indicated, noting the location and character of unexpected sounds. Assess heart rate and rhythm, peripheral color and temperature, pulses, edema, capillary refill in context, chest discomfort, urine output trends, and the client's mentation. New increased work of breathing, cyanosis, inability to speak normally, sudden chest pressure, weak perfusion, or rapidly changing vital signs require immediate focused action and appropriate help.

Neurologic, mobility, and skin assessment

Compare mental status with baseline and observe orientation, speech, pupils when indicated, strength, sensation, movement, gait, and balance. New facial asymmetry, unilateral weakness, a sudden speech change, decreased level of consciousness, or a new severe headache are time-sensitive cues. Protect the client from falls and activate the facility response while focused assessment continues.

Inspect skin across the person's actual skin tone for color change, bruising, wounds, rash, moisture, device pressure, and integrity. Palpate for temperature, tenderness, texture, edema, and changes around a wound or device. Areas over bony prominences, skin folds, the perineum, and under removable devices need intentional assessment. Do not rely on redness alone to detect early pressure-related injury across all skin tones; compare with surrounding skin and assess temperature, texture, tenderness, and nonblanching change according to policy.

Abdominal and elimination assessment

Ask about appetite, nausea, vomiting, bowel pattern, stool characteristics, flatus, urinary symptoms, continence, pain, and recent procedures. Inspect contour, distention, scars, tubes, drainage, and movement; then auscultate before percussion and palpation. If pain, rigidity, new distention, bleeding, persistent vomiting, or other concerning cues are present, assess the client and notify or escalate according to severity and policy. Do not repeatedly palpate a painful abdomen to prove a finding.

Lines, tubes, drains, and wounds

During every relevant assessment, trace a line from the client to the solution or device, verify the label and connections, observe insertion and surrounding skin, note patency or drainage, and check that ordered settings and alarms are appropriate. Never silence an unexplained alarm or manipulate equipment beyond preparation and policy. An unexpected device finding belongs in the same clinical picture as the client's symptoms and vital signs.

Turn data into a useful handoff

Document the time and conditions of assessment, relevant normal and abnormal findings, comparison with baseline, the client's own words, actions taken, notifications, and response. Avoid broad labels such as “neuro intact” or “lungs clear” without context when a focused finding matters. In a handoff, lead with the change and its urgency: “New right arm drift and slurred speech at 1010; baseline normal at 0800; stroke response activated.”

Clinical example

During a routine evening assessment, an RN notices that a client who walked independently earlier now uses the bedrail to sit up and speaks more slowly. The RN pauses the routine head-to-toe sequence, protects the client from falling, assesses level of consciousness, speech, strength, vital signs, oxygenation, glucose and other focused cues as indicated, compares with baseline, and activates the appropriate response. The value of the assessment is recognizing the change, not completing every checkbox.
